BETHESDA, Maryland (CNN) -- Josh Winston is a self-described problem solver. From his spacious office on the seventh floor of a high-rise building in Bethesda, Maryland, he fills out tax returns and keeps the books balanced for a number of his accounting clients. Josh Winston stands outside the 1983 RV he was converting to run on vegetable oil. "Everything on the left always equals everything on the right. For math-oriented people and musicians like me, that's very satisfying," he says. Four years ago, Winston was watching a late-night news program and saw a segment about converting diesel vehicles to run on alternative fuels. That night, Winston was hooked. He ordered a conversion kit for $900 and proceeded to convert a truck to run on used vegetable oil -- just to see if he could. Soon after, he converted his 1998 Jetta and affixed a sticker to the rear bumper that said, "This vehicle runs on straight vegetable oil." "For a single bumper sticker, I was surprised at how many people stopped me and said, 'Hey, how do you do that?' " Before taking on his first conversion, he hadn't worked on a car since his 1978 Plymouth Volare -- which he drove in college. By Winston's estimate, there are fewer than 10,000 vehicles on the road that have undergone these diesel conversions. Now, he sells and installs his own kits -- and he's the only person in the Washington, D.C., area to offer the service. Though his side business, named "Feed My Wheels dot com," has only converted a handful of vehicles, he recently took on his largest project by far -- a 1983 Itasca RV. "There's a lot of trial and error," says Winston.  Watch the "problem solver" at work » . Over the course of two days, Winston ran into many a problem. First, the batteries kept dying. Later, there was an issue with the alternator. By the end of Day 2, as Winston was preparing to fill a 40-gallon veggie-oil tank in the RV with recycled oil from a Chinese food restaurant, a neighbor watching him tipped over an 80-gallon holding tank, spilling tens of gallons of brown, smelly oil down his street. "It's OK," Winston quipped, "earthworms love this stuff." After nearly 50 hours of cutting and reattaching hoses, Winston managed to get the RV running and successfully switched over to the vegetable oil tank. He claims that veggie-oil emissions are about half of those of petroleum-based diesel fuel. "If you're emitting half the carbon dioxide that our neighbor is, that means one of two things: Either your neighbor can drive twice as much, or you're having a significant positive impact on the environment," Winston says. "In some small way, we're contributing to saving the environment. It's going to save a glacier somewhere."

# From Spreadsheets to Grease Traps: One Accountant's Alternative-Fuel Journey

Josh Winston never expected to spend his weekends elbow-deep in engine components. By day, he crunched numbers as an accountant, a profession defined by precision, predictability, and a distinct lack of grease under the fingernails. He had no mechanical training whatsoever—no childhood spent rebuilding carburetors with his father, no vocational classes, not even a passing familiarity with the difference between a fuel injector and a filter.

That all changed one sleepless night.

## The Spark

It happened during a bout of late-night channel surfing. A news segment flickered across his television screen, featuring a story about converting diesel engines to run on used vegetable oil—the kind of discarded fryer grease that restaurants pay to have hauled away. Something about the idea captured Winston's imagination. The notion that a waste product could power a vehicle felt almost too clever to be true.

Rather than letting the curiosity fade with the morning light, Winston dove in. He read forums, watched tutorials, ordered parts, and taught himself the mechanical skills he'd never possessed. Trial and error became his classroom, and slowly, methodically, he learned how to transform diesel vehicles into machines that ran on recycled cooking oil.

## Turning Passion into a Side Business

What began as a personal experiment eventually grew into something more. Winston launched a side business, giving it a name that captured both its purpose and its playful spirit: **"Feed My Wheels dot com."** The venture allowed him to share his newfound expertise, help other enthusiasts, and turn his unexpected hobby into a modest enterprise.

## The Itasca Challenge

His most ambitious undertaking to date has been the conversion of a 1983 Itasca RV—a project far larger and more complex than anything he'd attempted before. The vintage recreational vehicle tested every ounce of the knowledge he'd accumulated.

The setbacks came one after another. Batteries died without warning. The alternator gave him fits, presenting problems that would have discouraged a less determined tinkerer. Each obstacle demanded patience, troubleshooting, and a willingness to fail before succeeding. For a self-taught mechanic with an accountant's background, these challenges were formidable—but not insurmountable.

## A Movement in Its Infancy

Winston's persistence reflects something larger: a growing curiosity around alternative-fuel conversions. Across the country, more people are asking whether they can break free from conventional fuel dependence and power their vehicles with something more sustainable.

Yet the movement remains remarkably small. Fewer than 10,000 vehicles nationwide currently participate in this kind of alternative-fuel experiment—a tiny fraction of the vehicles on American roads. It's a niche pursuit, driven by hobbyists, environmentalists, and curious minds like Winston's.

For now, Josh Winston keeps working, one conversion at a time, proving that expertise isn't always inherited or formally taught. Sometimes, all it takes is a late-night spark of inspiration and the stubborn refusal to give up.

# The Bethesda Accountant Turning Fryer Grease Into Fuel

**BETHESDA, Maryland** — By day, Michael Reyes crunches numbers for small businesses across Montgomery County, poring over spreadsheets and quarterly tax filings from his tidy office suite. But on evenings and weekends, you're more likely to find him elbow-deep in an engine bay, the sharp tang of french fry oil hanging in the air.

Reyes, 47, is part accountant, part backyard chemist, and full-time evangelist for an unusual mission: converting diesel vehicles to run on used vegetable oil discarded by local restaurants.

"People think I'm joking when I tell them," Reyes said, wiping his hands on a rag stained with the residue of a thousand meals. "Then they smell my truck at a stoplight and ask why it smells like a food truck."

## From Balance Sheets to Biofuel

The journey began five years ago when Reyes, frustrated by fluctuating fuel prices and curious about sustainability, stumbled onto an online community of "grease car" enthusiasts.

"I'm an accountant. I think about cost per mile, return on investment," he said with a laugh. "The math just kept pulling me in. Free fuel? That's a spreadsheet I wanted to build."

What started as a single conversion on his own aging diesel pickup has grown into a modest side business. Reyes now installs conversion kits — secondary fuel tanks, heated fuel lines, and filtration systems — for a growing clientele of eco-conscious drivers throughout the D.C. suburbs.

The process isn't as simple as pouring oil into a gas tank. Diesel engines can run on vegetable oil, but the oil must be heated to reduce its thickness. Reyes's conversions allow vehicles to start on regular diesel, switch to vegetable oil once the engine warms, and purge the lines with diesel before shutdown.

## A Symbiotic Relationship With Local Kitchens

The fuel itself comes free — and Reyes has become a familiar figure at restaurant back doors across Bethesda.

"He's doing us a favor, honestly," said Elena Kowalski, manager at a nearby diner who supplies Reyes with used oil. "We used to pay to have it hauled away. Now he takes it, filters it, and drives around on it. It's a win-win."

Reyes collects the oil in repurposed containers, then filters and de-waters it in a setup in his garage that he sheepishly admits has tested his wife's patience.

"There was a learning curve," he said. "And a few spills. My neighbors have been very understanding."

## The Fine Print

True to his profession, Reyes is careful to note the legal complexities. Drivers using vegetable oil as fuel are technically required to pay road taxes normally collected at the diesel pump, and he encourages clients to register with the appropriate authorities.

"I'm not here to help anyone dodge taxes," he said. "I file honest returns for a living. This is about sustainability and independence, done the right way."

Experts caution that grease conversions aren't for everyone. Improper filtration can damage engines, and cold weather poses challenges. But for the right vehicle and a willing owner, the appeal is undeniable.

## More Than a Side Hustle

For Reyes, the venture has become about something larger than saved fuel costs.

"Every gallon I burn is a gallon that didn't get pumped out of the ground, and a gallon of waste that didn't get thrown out," he said. "There's something satisfying about closing that loop."

He estimates he's converted more than three dozen vehicles and helped divert thousands of gallons of waste oil from disposal.

As the sun set over his garage on a recent evening, Reyes fired up his truck, the engine settling into a smooth idle. The faint aroma of fried food drifted through the neighborhood.

"My clients tell me their kids love it," he said, grinning. "They say the exhaust smells like dinner."

*Reyes plans to host a free workshop this spring for anyone curious about the process — accountants especially welcome.*

# The Grease Monkey's Gambit: One Man's Two-Day Odyssey to Fuel Freedom

## A backyard mechanic's quest to run his vintage RV on the discards of America's fryers

---

When Dave Kellerman rolled his 1983 Itasca Sunflyer into his driveway last month, his neighbors assumed the retired HVAC technician had finally lost his mind. The RV—all 27 feet of faded brown and cream fiberglass—hadn't run reliably in three years. What they didn't know was that Kellerman had a plan, a garage full of tools, and roughly forty gallons of used cooking oil sourced from a Chinese restaurant two blocks away.

"Everybody's got a problem they think can't be fixed," Kellerman says, wiping his hands on a rag that has clearly given up any pretense of being clean. "I just don't believe that. There's always a way through."

## Day One: Optimism and Aluminum

The conversion began, as most of Kellerman's projects do, with too much coffee and a stack of printed forum posts from vegetable-oil enthusiasts. His goal was straightforward on paper: the Itasca's diesel engine could theoretically burn straight vegetable oil (SVO), but only if that oil was heated first to reduce its viscosity.

"Cold veggie oil is like maple syrup," he explains. "You can't ask an old injection system to atomize maple syrup. It'll choke."

The solution required a dual-tank system—starting the engine on diesel, switching to heated vegetable oil once warm, then purging the lines with diesel before shutdown. Kellerman spent the first morning mounting an auxiliary tank and running coolant lines to warm the oil.

Then came the first mishap.

"I drilled into the wrong bulkhead," he laughs. "Went right through into a storage compartment I'd forgotten was there. Nice quarter-inch hole looking straight at my wife's old camping chairs."

The afternoon brought a second complication. The heat exchanger he'd ordered arrived with the wrong fittings, forcing an improvised trip to three hardware stores and a lengthy negotiation with brass adapters that "did not want to cooperate."

By nightfall, Day One ended with the tank mounted, the lines partially run, and Kellerman's kitchen table converted into a workshop that his wife, Linda, described as "a crime scene involving spaghetti."

## Day Two: Filtration and Frustration

The second day centered on the oil itself. Used fryer grease is a mess of food particles, water, and questionable substances that no engine wants to see. Kellerman built a gravity filtration system from a repurposed water heater tank, cheesecloth, and increasingly fine filter media.

"That's where I really underestimated things," he admits. "I thought filtering would take an hour. It took five. And I still ended up with the world's worst-smelling driveway."

The most dramatic moment came during the first attempt to switch the engine over to vegetable oil. A loose clamp on the fuel line—Kellerman blames fatigue—sprayed warm oil across the engine bay.

"It looked like the RV was sweating salad dressing," he says. "I had to shut it all down, degrease everything, and start over. Lost about two hours and most of my dignity."

But by early evening, after tightening every fitting he could reach, Kellerman fired up the Itasca. It sputtered on diesel, warmed for several minutes, and then—at the flip of a dashboard switch he'd wired himself—transitioned to running entirely on recycled cooking oil.

"When it kept running, I actually yelled," he says. "Linda thought I'd hurt myself."

## The Payoff, and the Perspective

The converted RV now emits a faint aroma that Kellerman describes as "somewhere between french fries and an egg roll." He estimates his fuel cost has dropped to nearly nothing, since the restaurant is happy to give away oil it would otherwise pay to dispose of.

But for Kellerman, the appeal runs deeper than savings.

"We throw away billions of gallons of this stuff," he says. "It gets hauled off, sometimes dumped, sometimes rendered. Meanwhile, it's got real energy still in it. Reusing it feels like closing a loop that never should've been open."

He's careful not to oversell the environmental math. Veggie oil isn't carbon-free—the crops require farming, and the diesel used for startup and purging is still petroleum. Older engines also produce their own emissions concerns.

"I'm not claiming I saved the planet with a Chinese restaurant's leftover grease," he says. "But I kept forty gallons of waste out of the trash and drove on it. That's not nothing. And it beats letting a good RV rot."

## The Bigger Idea

What Kellerman seems most eager to share isn't the technical recipe—it's the mindset.

"People look at an old RV, an old problem, an old habit, and they think 'that's just how it is,'" he says, gesturing at the Itasca now idling contentedly on discarded oil. "But most things can be fixed, reused, or rethought. You just have to be stubborn enough to try, and dumb enough not to quit when you drill through the wrong wall."

He plans to take the Itasca on a coast-to-coast trip this summer, stopping at restaurants along the way to top off his tank.

"Free fuel, good stories, and a machine that shouldn't be running but is," he grins. "That's about as good as it gets."

---

*Dave Kellerman documents his projects on a modest personal blog, where the veggie-oil conversion post has already drawn questions from would-be tinkerers across the country. His advice to all of them is the same: "Buy more hose clamps than you think you need. Trust me."*

# The Numbers Man: How a Late-Night Broadcast Turned a Math Enthusiast into a Fuel Conversion Entrepreneur

**By [Staff Writer]**

The garage behind Dale Kowalski's modest ranch house doesn't look like the headquarters of a growing business. Fluorescent tubes hum overhead, casting light on workbenches cluttered with copper tubing, pressure gauges, and stacks of graph paper covered in his cramped, deliberate handwriting. A whiteboard on the far wall displays a tangle of equations that would give most people a headache.

To Kowalski, 54, they're the most beautiful thing in the room.

"Everything comes back to the numbers," he says, tapping the marker against a figure representing thermal efficiency. "People think alternative fuel is about politics or saving the planet. For me? It started as a math problem I couldn't stop thinking about."

## A Sleepless Beginning

The problem found him five years ago, during a bout of insomnia that had become routine after his job at a regional accounting firm downsized his department to part-time.

"I was up at two in the morning, flipping channels," he recalls, settling onto a stool worn smooth from years of use. "There was this news segment—some guy in the Midwest running his truck on used cooking oil from a diner. The reporter was doing the whole 'can you believe it' angle. But I wasn't listening to the story. I was doing the math in my head."

The economics, as he calculated them, seemed almost too favorable to be true. Within a week, Kowalski had filled three notebooks with energy content comparisons, viscosity calculations, and cost projections.

"My wife thought I'd lost it," he laughs. "I'd always been the guy who did puzzles, who read books about prime numbers for fun. Suddenly I'm ordering fuel samples and arguing with strangers on forums about combustion ratios."

## From Curiosity to Craft

What separated Kowalski from the thousands of others who watch such segments and forget them by morning was persistence—and a temperament suited to slow, methodical problem-solving.

His first conversion, performed on a 1998 diesel sedan he bought for $800, took four months and failed twice.

"The first attempt, I gelled the fuel lines in cold weather. Basic mistake. But that's the thing about math—when something goes wrong, there's always a reason. You just have to find the variable you missed."

He kept meticulous records of every trial: temperatures, fuel blends, mileage, engine performance. The spreadsheets grew into a database, and the database became, unexpectedly, a business.

"People started asking me to convert their vehicles. Then they wanted to do it themselves. That's when I realized the real product wasn't the conversion—it was the knowledge, packaged so anyone could use it."

## The Kit

Today, Kowalski's conversion kits sell for between $400 and $1,200, depending on the vehicle. Each ships with hardware, custom-fitted components, and what he considers the crown jewel: a thick instruction manual he wrote himself, complete with the calculations behind every recommendation.

"Other companies just tell you to bolt part A to part B," he says with mild disdain. "I explain *why*. If you understand the thermodynamics, you can troubleshoot anything. You're not dependent on me."

That philosophy has earned him a devoted, if niche, customer base. He sells roughly 30 to 40 kits a month, mostly to rural customers, small-scale farmers, and fellow tinkerers drawn to the self-sufficiency of it all.

He's quick to manage expectations, though. A laminated card on his desk lists disclaimers about warranties, emissions regulations, and local laws.

"I'm not selling a miracle. I tell everyone: check your regulations, understand your vehicle, know what you're getting into. This isn't for people who want to push a button and forget about it."

## The Skeptics and the Reality

Critics of home fuel conversions point to potential engine damage, warranty voids, and inconsistent emissions performance. Kowalski doesn't dismiss these concerns—he engages them with the same rigor he applies to everything.

"Are there risks? Absolutely. Can you damage an engine if you do it wrong? Yes. That's exactly why the education matters more than the parts." He pulls out a binder of customer correspondence, much of it troubleshooting advice he provides free of charge. "I'd rather talk someone out of a sale than sell them something they'll misuse."

Industry observers note that hobbyist conversions occupy a legal gray area that varies significantly by state, and that the environmental benefits—often the initial draw—can be more modest than enthusiasts assume once the full lifecycle is calculated.

Kowalski, characteristically, has run those numbers too.

"Am I saving the world? No. But for the right person, with the right situation, the math works. And there's something honest about that."

## Still Just a Hobby, Sort Of

Despite the steady income, Kowalski resists calling himself an entrepreneur. The business remains, in his mind, an extension of the puzzle that captured him that sleepless night.

"I still keep accounting hours part-time. This isn't about getting rich—it never was. It's about the problem. There's always a way to squeeze out another percent of efficiency, another dollar of savings. I'll probably be chasing that number until they carry me out of this garage."

He glances back at the whiteboard, at the equations that started it all.

"Most people saw a novelty on the news. I saw a question I hadn't answered yet." He shrugs. "Five years later, I'm still answering it."

Outside, the converted sedan—now on its fourth engine and hundreds of thousands of miles—sits in the driveway, ready for another data point.

---

*[This profile is a fictional composite intended to illustrate the journalistic profile format. Readers interested in fuel conversions should consult local regulations and qualified professionals, as such modifications carry legal, safety, and warranty implications.]*

# From Fryer to Freeway: How One D.C. Man Turned His Diesel Into a Veggie-Powered Machine

**By CNN Staff**

ARLINGTON, Virginia — On a crisp Saturday morning, Marcus Delaney pops the hood of his 2003 Volkswagen Jetta and points to an additional tank nestled where a spare tire once sat. The faint smell wafting from his exhaust isn't diesel fumes—it's something closer to a fast-food kitchen.

"People roll down their windows at stoplights and ask if I'm cooking french fries," Delaney says with a laugh. "I tell them, not quite—but they're not far off."

Delaney, 41, is part of a small but growing community of enthusiasts across the Washington, D.C., region who have converted their diesel vehicles to run on used vegetable oil, the same grease that once fried onion rings and chicken tenders at local restaurants.

## A Movement Fueled by Frustration—and Grease

The practice, sometimes called "greasing," involves modifying a diesel engine to burn straight vegetable oil (SVO) or waste vegetable oil (WVO) collected from restaurants. While the technology has existed for decades, rising fuel costs and environmental concerns have breathed new life into the niche hobby.

"I started three years ago when gas prices spiked," Delaney explains, gesturing toward the modest heating system he installed to thin the oil before it reaches the engine. "I did the math and thought, why am I paying at the pump when restaurants are practically giving this stuff away?"

Delaney estimates he's saved thousands of dollars since converting his car, spending roughly $1,200 on the initial conversion kit and installation. Now, he collects used oil from three restaurants near his Arlington home—free of charge—filtering it in his garage before filling his tank.

## Not as Simple as Pouring Oil In

Experts caution that the process requires significant technical knowledge and commitment.

"You can't just dump cooking oil into any car," says Dr. Elena Vasquez, an automotive engineering researcher who has studied alternative fuels. "It only works with diesel engines, and even then, vegetable oil is thicker than diesel. It needs to be heated, and the vehicle typically starts on regular diesel before switching over."

There are legal considerations too. Federal and state regulations require road-use fuel taxes to be paid, meaning enthusiasts like Delaney are technically supposed to report their veggie oil mileage and pay the appropriate taxes—a rule many hobbyists admit is inconsistently followed and enforced.

## Building a Community

For Delaney, the appeal goes beyond savings. He's become an informal ambassador, hosting monthly meetups where curious newcomers learn the basics of filtering, storage, and engine modification.

"It's a community of tinkerers, environmentalists, and frugal folks," he says. "Some people come for the savings, some for the planet, some just because they love the challenge."

The environmental benefits, while real, are modest and debated. Burning used vegetable oil can reduce reliance on fossil fuels and repurposes waste, but critics note that the practice can't scale to meaningful levels—there simply isn't enough used cooking oil to power a significant portion of vehicles.

"It's a solution for individuals, not for society," Vasquez says. "But that doesn't make it any less meaningful for the people doing it."

## The Road Ahead

As electric vehicles increasingly dominate the alternative-fuel conversation, some wonder whether veggie-oil conversions are a fading novelty. Delaney isn't worried.

"Electric is great, but not everyone can afford a new EV," he says, wiping grease from his hands. "This is accessible. It's hands-on. And honestly, there's something satisfying about driving on fuel you filtered yourself in your own garage."

As he closes the hood and climbs into the driver's seat, Delaney offers a final thought.

"People think I'm crazy," he says, starting the engine with a familiar diesel rumble. "But when I drive past a gas station without stopping, I feel pretty smart."

He pulls out of the driveway, leaving behind the faint, unmistakable scent of a fryer on the open road.

---

*Have a story about unconventional fuels or DIY engineering? CNN wants to hear from you.*

# Local Man's RV Runs on Sweet-and-Sour Fumes, Saves Planet One Egg Roll at a Time

*Retired mechanic converts vintage motorhome to run on recycled cooking oil—and he's never smelled better*

---

**RIVERSIDE** — When Gary Pemberton fires up his 1987 Winnebago, the neighbors don't reach for their earplugs. They reach for their chopsticks.

That's because Pemberton, a 61-year-old retired diesel mechanic, has spent the last eight months converting his beloved recreational vehicle to run entirely on used cooking oil sourced from the Golden Dragon, a family-owned Chinese restaurant just three blocks from his home.

"People think I'm nuts until they hear the engine purr," Pemberton said, wiping his hands on a rag that smelled faintly of sesame. "Then they just think I'm hungry."

## From Wok to Wheels

The conversion process, Pemberton explained, involves a filtration system he cobbled together in his garage, along with a heating element that keeps the thicker vegetable oil flowing smoothly through the fuel lines. Diesel engines, it turns out, are surprisingly forgiving about what you feed them.

"Rudolf Diesel actually designed his original engine to run on peanut oil back in 1900," Pemberton noted with the enthusiasm of a man who has cornered many a dinner guest with this exact fact. "So really, I'm the traditionalist here."

Every week, Pemberton collects roughly 40 gallons of spent fryer oil that the Golden Dragon would otherwise pay to dispose of. It's a win-win arrangement.

"Before, we call company, they take oil away, we pay money," said restaurant owner Lin Chen, laughing. "Now Gary takes it, we save money, and he brings us tomatoes from his garden. Much better deal."

## Saving Glaciers, One Fry Basket at a Time

Pemberton is quick to steer the conversation toward the environmental benefits, a topic he approaches with the zeal of the newly converted.

"You know how much carbon a regular diesel engine pumps out? This is basically carbon-neutral," he said, gesturing broadly at his rig. "The plants that made this oil already pulled CO2 out of the air. I'm just borrowing it for a while."

Then, pausing dramatically, he added: "Every mile I drive on egg-roll oil is a mile that isn't melting some glacier up in Greenland. I like to think there's a polar bear out there who owes me a thank-you card."

While experts note that used cooking oil isn't a perfect solution—there simply isn't enough fryer grease in the world to fuel every vehicle—recycling waste oil that would otherwise be discarded does genuinely reduce emissions and keeps grease out of landfills and sewer systems.

## The One Small Catch

There is, admittedly, one side effect Pemberton has learned to embrace.

"My wife says the whole RV smells like a food court," he chuckled. "I've stopped fighting it. I just keep a fortune cookie in the cup holder and call it ambiance."

His grandkids, apparently, are big fans of road trips now.

"They used to complain about being carsick," he said. "Now they just get carhungry."

## The Road Ahead

Pemberton has plans to log 5,000 miles this summer on a cross-country trip, and he intends to document his fuel stops at restaurants along the way—not for gasoline, but for grease.

"Some folks collect postcards," he said. "I'm gonna collect grease traps."

As for the skeptics who question whether one man's fry-oil Winnebago can really make a difference?

Pemberton just smiled and patted the hood of his humming, faintly aromatic machine.

"Maybe not," he admitted. "But if everybody did one small crazy thing for the planet, we'd be in a lot better shape. Besides—" he added with a grin, "I get 22 miles to the gallon and I never have to stop for lunch."

---

*The Golden Dragon has since added a sign to its window: "Now Fueling Cars AND Customers."*
